title: AAO Non-Precedent Decision — Application for T Nonimmigrant Status (2025-11-12)
text:
U.S. Citizenship Non-Precedent Decision of the
and Immigration Administrative Appeals Office
Services
In Re: 39715629 Date: NOVEMBER 12, 2025
Appeal of Service Center Operations (SCOPS) Decision
Form 1-914, Application for T Nonimmigrant Status
The Applicant seeks T-1 nonimmigrant classification as a victim of human trafficking under sections
101(a)(15)(T) and 214(0) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (the Act), 8 U.S.C. sections
1101(a)(15)(T) and 1184(0).
Service Center Operations (SCOPS) denied the application, concluding that the Applicant did not
submit a valid application or supporting documents due to signature deficiencies. The matter is now
before us on appeal pursuant to 8 C.F.R. § 103.3.
The Applicant bears the burden ofproof to demonstrate eligibility by a preponderance of the evidence.
Matter ofChawathe, 25 I&N Dec. 369, 375-76 (AAO 2010). We review the questions in this matter
de novo. Matter of Christo 's, Inc., 26 l&N Dec. 537, 537 n.2 (AAO 2015). Upon de novo review,
we will dismiss the appeal.
After receiving the Applicant's Form 1-914, Application for T Nonimmigrant Status (T application),
SCOPS issued a request for evidence (RFE) informing the Applicant that his T application did not
appear to be a copy of a document personally signed by the Applicant and therefore did not conform
to signature requirements. In the decision denying the application, SCOPS noted that the appearance
of the Applicant's signature was exactly the same on multiple documents, which was the functional
equivalent of a stamp. The Applicant's RFE response included a second application form, but did not
include the original or copy of the T application the Applicant originally submitted. The Applicant
had therefore not shown that he personally signed his T application prior to filing.
On appeal, the Applicant asserts that he properly submitted his original application because the
documents he submitted included an electronically reproduced copy of his original handwritten
signature. 1 He contends that guidance provided by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
(USCIS) indicates that signatures are considered valid even if the original signature on the document
is a "photocopied, scanned, faxed, or similarly reproduced" copy ofthe original handwritten signature.
Moreover, the Applicant states that his RFE response cured the deficiencies in the original application.
Furthermore, he argues that SCOPS' denial ofhis application for the signature deficiencies stems from
1 On appeal, the Applicant submits a third application form, dated June 6, 2025, but the record does not contain the original
application with a handwritten signature, as requested.

an overly formalistic, technical interpretation of the regulations and raises due process concerns for a
vulnerable individual who should benefit from a victim-centered approach and whose application was
pending for over a year. The Applicant requests that we exercise discretion to accept his application
for these reasons.
Upon de novo review, the Applicant has not overcome the reasons for the denial of his T application.
The Applicant's signature appears to have been copied and pasted or created by a stamp or similar
device for use on multiple documents. This is not acceptable as a valid signature because the
regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(a)(2) specifies that non-electronic applications require "handwritten"
signatures, which include the instant application. Applicants are required to sign their benefit requests.
Id.
We discern no distinction between a digitally "cut and paste" signature and the simulated signatures
created by word processor, stamp, auto-pen, or similar device, as they all may be used to replicate a
person's signature without their direct involvement in the act of signing. Each format may be created
or applied by someone other than the signatory, in violation of 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(a)(2). In this case,
the signature is invalid because it does not signify the purported signatory knows the contents of the
request and supporting documents submitted on their behalf, that they have reviewed and approved of
the information therein, and that they have certified the truth and correctness of the request under
penalty of perjury. See Form I-914, Part 6.
The probative force of a benefit request subscribed under penalty of perjury derives from the actual
signature of the applicant or petitioner. 28 U.S.C. § 1746 (requiring the signature of the declarant);
see also U.S. v. Bueno-Vargas, 383 F.3d 1104, 1111 (9th Cir. 2004) ("We conclude that signing a
statement under penalty ofperjury satisfies the standard for an oath or affirmation, as it is a signal that
the declarant understands the legal significance of the declarant's statements and the potential for
punishment if the declarant lies."). By requiring an applicant or petitioner to verify the truth of the
benefit request, the submitted evidence, and the related claims by personally reviewing and signing
the immigration form under penalty ofperjury, USCIS aims to ensure the accuracy of the information.
Only the applicant or petitioner can attest to the truth of these matters. When a USCIS f01m is not
signed by the applicant or petitioner to attest to its veracity, the evidentiary basis for the application
or petition and supporting evidence no longer exists.
Additionally, the signature requirement safeguards the protections accorded an applicant or petitioner
under 8 U.S.C. § 1367 ("Penalties for disclosure of information"), as required in the current
matter. See also 8 C.F.R. § 214.216 (setting f01ih restrictions on the use and disclosure of inf01mation
relating to T applicants). The signature on a T application authorizes the release of protected privacy
information in limited circumstances that, if erroneous, could endanger the applicant and violate
privacy laws. See 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(b)(16) ("Inspection of evidence"); see also Form I-914, Pati 6.
The Applicant further asserts that his filing is consistent with the intent of regulations, yet he does not
claim, nor has he demonstrated, that he personally signed the documents initially submitted with the
T application. The Applicant cannot cure this by later submitting an additional application associated
with the same filing. An applicant may not make material changes to an application that has already
been filed in an effort to make a deficient application conform to USCIS requirements. Matter of
Izummi, 22 I&N Dec. 169, 175 (Assoc. Comm'r 1998).
2

Although we acknowledge the difficulties the Applicant claims he will face as a result of the adverse
finding in his case here, we lack the authority to waive or disregard any of the Act's requirements, as
implemented by regulation. See United States v. Nixon, 418 U.S. 683,695 (1974) (providing that "[s]o
long as this regulation is extant it has the force oflaw"). Moreover, SCOPS' decision was procedurally
appropriate despite the Applicant's concern that the application was first accepted and later denied.
The review and analysis of a questionable signature is an adjudication itself and it is appropriate to
deny a benefit request when it is not properly signed under penalty of perjury.
In conclusion, the Applicant has not overcome the reasons for the denial on appeal and the application
will remain denied. Furthermore, this decision is without prejudice to any application the Applicant
may wish to file in the future. 2
ORDER: The appeal is dismissed.
NOTICE: This constitutes the final decision in this matter. The filing of a motion will not postpone the
effect of the decision. 8 C.F.R. § 103.S(a)(l)(iv). Aliens who are not lawfully present, or who are
otherwise inadmissible or deportable, may be subject to the commencement of removal proceedings
under section 240 ofthe Act through the issuance of a Form I-862, Notice to Appear. Those proceedings
may result in their removal from the United States and possible ineligibility for future visas or other
immigration benefits.
2 SCOPS also dete1mined that the Applicant has not established that he: has been a victim of a severe form of trafficking
in persons; is physically present in the United States on account of such trafficking; would suffer extreme hardship upon
removal from the United States; and is admissible to the United States. Because the Applicant did not submit a valid
application, we need not reach, and therefore reserve, these issues. See INS v. Bagamasbad, 429 U.S. 24, 25 (1976) (per
curiam) (holding that agencies are not required to make "purely advisory findings" on issues that are unnecessary to the
ultimate decision).
